lead: A thermometer needs a scale, and gas thermometers using different gases disagree slightly. The thermodynamic temperature scale removes the working substance from the definition. Carnot's theorem says every reversible engine between the same two reservoirs has the same heat ratio, so that ratio can define temperature. We set T₁/T₂ = Q₁/Q₂. This makes Carnot efficiency exactly 1 − T₂/T₁ for every substance. The scale is used whenever second-law calculations need absolute temperatures, such as entropy and exergy, and it fixes the Kelvin scale.
prereq: You need: 3.4 Carnot cycle and Carnot's theorem and Unit 1, Foundations: Systems, Properties and Zeroth Law (temperature and the zeroth law).

sections.h3: Why a gas scale is not enough

blocks.text: A gas thermometer reads temperature by a gas property, for example pressure at fixed volume. It assumes p/p<sub>tr</sub> = T/T<sub>tr</sub>, where p is the gas pressure, p<sub>tr</sub> is the pressure at the triple point, T is the temperature to be found, and T<sub>tr</sub> is 273.16 K. Different gases do not follow this relation exactly. Readings from helium, nitrogen and argon agree closely near the ideal-gas range and drift apart outside it. A fundamental scale cannot depend on which gas is inside the bulb.

Carnot's theorem, from 3.4, removes the gas. Every reversible engine working between the same two reservoirs has the same thermal efficiency η, where η = W/Q₁, W is work output and Q₁ is heat taken from the hot reservoir. The theorem holds for any working substance: gas, steam, or a magnetic material. So the heat ratio Q₁/Q₂ of a reversible engine is a property of the two reservoirs only, not of the engine. That ratio is the raw material for a substance-free temperature scale.

The practical problem is small but serious. A thermometer calibrated with one gas can disagree with a thermometer calibrated with another gas by amounts that matter in careful work. Metrology needs one scale that every thermometer realises, not a family of gas-dependent scales.

sections.h3: Defining temperature by a reversible engine

blocks.text: Take a reversible engine between a hot reservoir at thermodynamic temperature T₁ and a cold reservoir at T₂. Let Q₁ be heat taken from the hot reservoir and Q₂ be heat rejected to the cold reservoir, both as positive magnitudes in joule. Carnot's theorem says Q₁/Q₂ is fixed by the two reservoirs. Define temperature so that the same ratio holds:

blocks.where: T₁ and T₂ are thermodynamic temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs, in kelvin; Q₁ is heat taken from the hot reservoir by a reversible engine, in joule; Q₂ is heat rejected to the cold reservoir, in joule.

blocks.text: This is the thermodynamic temperature scale. It is also called the Kelvin scale. The definition uses only heat quantities, which are measured with a calorimeter or from work and first-law balances. It never asks what the engine contains. If a reversible engine takes 600 J from a hot reservoir and rejects 300 J to a cold reservoir, then T₁/T₂ = 600/300 = 2. The hot reservoir is twice as hot as the cold one on this scale.

items: Only ratios are fixed. Multiplying every T by a constant leaves every Q₁/Q₂ unchanged.
One fixed point is needed. The triple point of water is assigned 273.16 K exactly.
With this fixed point, the scale is fixed completely and is written in kelvin, symbol K.

blocks.text: The scale coincides with the ideal-gas scale. For an ideal gas, a reversible Carnot cycle gives Q₁/Q₂ = T₁/T₂ when T is the ideal-gas temperature. So gas thermometer readings need no correction when they are treated as thermodynamic temperatures. The agreement is exact for an ideal gas and is the reason the Kelvin scale looks familiar.
For a reversible engine, the first law gives W = Q₁ − Q₂. Thermal efficiency is η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁. Insert the defining ratio Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁:

blocks.where: η<sub>rev</sub> is the thermal efficiency of a reversible engine, dimensionless; T₁ is the hot-reservoir temperature, in kelvin; T₂ is the cold-reservoir temperature, in kelvin.

blocks.text: This result is exact for every reversible engine, whatever the working substance. For a real engine between the same reservoirs, η is lower. The reversible value is the yardstick. It is not a prediction of a real engine's efficiency; see 3.6 for how irreversibility enters.

η = 1 would need T₂/T₁ = 0, so T₂ = 0 K. Absolute zero is not available. The third law says it cannot be reached in a finite number of steps. Every real engine with a sink above 0 K rejects some heat, so its efficiency is below 100%.

The definition also sets the zero: T = 0 K is the lower limit of the scale. It is approached, never reached. Temperatures in °C are shifted Kelvin values: T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15. Use kelvin in every second-law formula.

figure.caption: Efficiency of a reversible engine against source temperature for sinks at 300 K and 600 K. The colder sink gives the higher curve; both approach one as T₁ grows, but never reach it at finite T₁.

spec.aria: Efficiency rises towards one as the source temperature grows, and the curve for the colder sink of 300 K lies above the curve for the 600 K sink.

examples.question: Two reversible engines work in series. The first takes heat from a source at T₁ and rejects it at T₂. The second takes that heat at T₂ and rejects it at 300 K. Each engine has a thermal efficiency of 20%. Find T₁ and T₂ on the thermodynamic scale.
steps: Write the reversible efficiency for the second engine: η₂ = 1 − T<sub>L</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> = 1 − 300 K / T₂.
Write the reversible efficiency for the first engine: η₁ = 1 − T₂/T₁ = 1 − 375 K / T₁.

Check the heat ratios. For engine 1, Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁ = 375/468.75 = 0.80. For engine 2, Q₃/Q₂ = 300/375 = 0.80, where Q₃ is heat rejected to 300 K. Both engines reject 80% of the heat they receive, as a 20% efficiency requires.
examples.answer: T₂ = 375 K and T₁ = 468.75 K on the thermodynamic scale.

traps: T₁/T₂ = Q₁/Q₂ applies only to a reversible engine. A real engine's heat ratio is not a temperature ratio.
Use absolute temperatures in kelvin. Substituting 27 for 300 K in a second-law formula gives a meaningless answer.
The definition fixes only ratios. Without the triple-point value 273.16 K, all temperatures could be multiplied by an arbitrary constant.
Efficiency 100% needs T₂ = 0 K exactly. A very small sink temperature still gives η below 1.
Do not use the Carnot formula to predict a real engine's efficiency. It is the upper limit, not the actual value.

quiz.q: State the defining relation of the thermodynamic temperature scale for a reversible engine.
quiz.a: T₁/T₂ = Q₁/Q₂, where T₁ and T₂ are thermodynamic temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs, and Q₁ and Q₂ are heat taken and rejected by a reversible engine, both positive.

quiz.q: Why does the thermodynamic scale not need a particular gas?
quiz.a: Carnot's theorem makes Q₁/Q₂ of a reversible engine depend only on the two reservoirs. The definition uses this heat ratio, not any gas property.

quiz.q: A reversible engine works between 500 K and 300 K. Find its efficiency and the ratio Q₂/Q₁.
Two reversible engines in series between T₁ and 300 K each have efficiency 25%. Find T₁.
quiz.a: Second engine: 0.25 = 1 − 300/T₂, so T₂ = 400 K. First engine: 0.25 = 1 − 400/T₁, so T₁ = 400/0.75 = 533.33 K.

quiz.q: Why is one fixed point necessary on the thermodynamic scale?
quiz.a: The definition fixes only ratios T₁/T₂. Without a fixed numerical value at one known temperature, all temperatures can be scaled by an arbitrary constant.

quiz.q: For a reversible engine with source at 600 K and sink at 300 K, find η.
Can a reversible engine reach η = 100% if the sink is at 0.001 K? Explain.
quiz.a: No. η = 1 − T₂/T₁, so η = 1 needs T₂ = 0 K exactly. At 0.001 K the efficiency is below 1. Absolute zero is not attainable.

quiz.q: What is the fixed point of the Kelvin scale and its value?
quiz.a: The triple point of water, 273.16 K.

beyond: Not for the exam. The thermodynamic scale is the basis of the kelvin in metrology. Modern thermometry realises the kelvin through defined fixed points and interpolation instruments, not through a real Carnot engine. The 2019 SI redefinition fixes the kelvin by the Boltzmann constant, but the thermodynamic scale remains the reference. Cryogenics, aerospace and exergy analysis all use absolute temperatures because second-law formulas need ratios. Search next for the International Temperature Scale, the triple point of water, and Carnot-limited efficiency.
